analysis.one_liner: Caps Medicare drug cost-sharing at the drug's net price after rebates or its pharmacy cash price, whichever is lower.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared a House committee without a single dissenting vote, 45-0, but was never brought to the House floor and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under Medicare's drug benefit, seniors in the coverage gap often pay cost-sharing based on a drug's inflated list price, even when insurers receive large rebates that make the real price much lower. This bill would cap what a Medicare beneficiary pays per month's supply at the drug's average net price after rebates, or the pharmacy's cash price if that is lower, starting in 2027. It also caps copays for low-income beneficiaries the same way and directs the Government Accountability Office to report on whether plans comply.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who take prescription drugs: once they pass the deductible, their monthly cost-sharing could not exceed the drug's average net price after rebates or the pharmacy's cash price, whichever is lower. Low-income beneficiaries get a matching cap on their copays.

how_it_helps.text: Starting in plan year 2027, cost-sharing for a month's supply of a covered Part D drug, after the deductible and before the out-of-pocket threshold, cannot exceed the drug's average net price (amount paid less rebates) or the pharmacy's cash price, whichever is lower.
The bill applies the same cap to Medicare Advantage drug coverage through the Part D provisions, per the CRS summary.
For plan year 2027 onward, copays for low-income beneficiaries may not exceed the same net-price cap.
The Comptroller General must report to Congress by January 1, 2029 on compliance and enforcement, with recommendations for public disclosure and awareness.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare drug plans and the pharmacy benefit managers and drug manufacturers behind the rebate system would collect less in cost-sharing, since enrollee payments would be based on post-rebate net prices rather than inflated list prices. Any shift in plan costs could flow back into premiums or Medicare spending.
analysis.who_pays_short: Part D plans and rebate middlemen

drawbacks.text: The mechanism relies on plan-reported 'average net price' calculations, which are hard for beneficiaries to verify; that is likely why the bill directs the GAO to study compliance and enforcement rather than building an enforcement mechanism up front.

The cap takes effect in 2027 and only covers the phase between the deductible and the out-of-pocket threshold, so beneficiaries' first-dollar costs before the deductible, and costs above the threshold, are not affected.

If plans cannot recover cost-sharing dollars in this phase, they may recoup through premiums or benefit design, an honest supporter would have to acknowledge this trade-off; the GAO report was intended to surface such effects only after implementation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is straightforward and consumer-protective: people should not pay cost-sharing on a price the plan does not actually pay after rebates. Its weaknesses are that it is narrow (one coverage phase, effective 2027) and leans on after-the-fact GAO review rather than a strong enforcement design. On balance it is a modest, well-targeted consumer protection whose main defect is how small and delayed it is.

outcome.mechanism: It won unanimous approval in the House Energy and Commerce Committee but House leadership never scheduled it for a floor vote, and it died when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Nicole Malliotakis introduced the bill with Rep. Brad Wenstrup on July 25, 2023; it was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees.
The Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee considered and marked it up on November 15, 2023, forwarding it to the full committee by voice vote.
On December 6, 2023, the full Energy and Commerce Committee ordered the bill reported, as amended, by a vote of 45-0.

After committee approval, the bill received no further floor action; on December 17, 2024 it was referred back to the Subcommittee on Health, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with no House vote ever taken.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Part D plans, pharmacy benefit managers, and manufacturers keep the current arrangement in which beneficiary cost-sharing is calculated off rebate-inflated list prices; seniors' drug cost-sharing stays on the old, higher basis.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Part D plans, PBMs, and drug makers

industries.industry: Medicare drug plans and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: Plans' cost-sharing would be capped at post-rebate net prices instead of list prices, cutting the gap between what enrollees pay and what plans actually pay. The bill died before that arrangement had to change.

Rebates they pay are already reflected in the net-price cap, so their net revenues change little, but beneficiaries' cost-sharing tied to inflated list prices falls. The main financial impact lands on the plans and middlemen, not manufacturers directly.
